**Final search score: 49.07× faster than the reference, using 4 of the 24 scorer calls.** The answer is in `final.py`. I don't have a score on the unseen instances. On harness seeds I never tuned on it was 47.4× faster, and it matched the reference exactly on 3,000 small edge-case tests.

| Candidate | What changed | Local harness | Official search score |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline | — | 1× | ~1.0 |
| A (first working version) | prefix sums + binary search | 36.1× | 32.24 |
| B | merge all start/end points in one dict | 28.3× | dropped |
| C | faster sorts (by one field, not whole tuples), searches run in C | 41.7× | 41.23 |
| D | all per-window arithmetic in C-level `map`/`itemgetter` | 44.6× | 44.84 |
| E | reuse the start-side search results for the count | 46.1× | — |
| **F = final** | sort by end starting from the start-sorted list | 47.8× | **49.07** |

**Why it's faster:** the reference checks every session against every window. Instead, for any time `t`, I define `F(t)` = the rate-weighted session time before `t`. Two sorted lists (starts, ends) with running totals of `rate` and `rate × start` (or end) give `F(t)` with two binary searches. Each window's usage is then `F(hi) − F(lo)`. Its count is the number of sessions starting before `hi` minus the number ending at or before `lo`; no session is subtracted wrongly, because none can start at or after `hi` and also end at or before `lo`. Everything stays in exact integers, and the order of the results is unchanged. The cost drops from sessions × windows to sorting plus a few searches per window. About 0.7 ms of the roughly 1.7 ms that remains is the two sorts.

**Process:** I followed the evolve skill. I built a local harness: an exact-match check against the reference on 3,000 small cases (empty inputs, duplicate sessions, negative rates, huge rates), plus timing on about 4,000 sessions and 400 windows. Its rankings matched the official scorer at every point I checked (36 vs 32, 41.7 vs 41.2, 44.6 vs 44.8). I stopped with budget left because the last round's changes were each only about 5%, and the remaining time is mostly the sort, which I don't see a way to cut.

**One thing to know about F:** its gain over E (about 7% here) depends on the data. It helps when sessions are short compared with the overall time span, because then sorting by end is close to sorting by start. With long sessions it should be about as fast as E, not slower.

I left helper files in the folder: `harness.py`, `prof.py`, `prof2.py` and `cand_*.py`.
